text_full:
1 terrorist killed in Kulgam encounter, injured Lashkar commander likely escaped
This comes a day after security forces launched a cordon and search operation in the district following inputs about the presence of terrorists responsible for the attack on a CRPF post last week.
One terrorist was killed in an encounter with security forces in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam on Monday, while another managed to escape, possibly in an injured condition, officials said. Only one body has so far been recovered from the encounter site and the identification process is underway.
There is a strong possibility that wanted Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) operative Lateef Bhat, suspected to be involved in the attack on a CRPF post in Kulgam last week, escaped the encounter site in an injured condition, officials said. Security forces continue to hunt for the Lashkar local commander, with the area remaining under a tight cordon.
According to preliminary identification, the killed terrorist has been identified as Umar. Further details about him are yet to be disclosed by officials. His body was recovered along with a suspected AK-series rifle found in his possession.
Meanwhile, an extensive anti-militancy operation across rural Kulgam has entered its sixth consecutive day, with security forces conducting intensive door-to-door searches across more than 15 villages in the south Kashmir district following the November 11 ambush on a CRPF patrol party.
Joint teams of the Army, Jammu and Kashmir Police and the CRPF have maintained a tight security grid around the cordoned areas. Residential houses, outhouses, orchards and dense foliage are being thoroughly searched to track down the attackers and identify possible hideouts.
Drones, sniffer dogs and metal detectors have also been deployed as part of the sweeping search operation. Security personnel have established multiple checkpoints along entry and exit points, restricting civilian movement while verification drives continue.
More than 600 suspects have been questioned so far, while several people have been detained as part of the ongoing investigation. Residents in the cordoned villages are also being questioned as security forces intensify their searches.
Gunshots were also heard during search operations in Laroo village of Kulgam, prompting security forces to rush reinforcements to the location. Two Lashkar terrorists were initially believed to be trapped in the area, triggering an exchange of fire.
The operations are being carried out jointly by the Jammu and Kashmir Police's Special Operations Group (SOG), the 18th Battalion of the CRPF and the Army's Rashtriya Rifles (RR).
The encounter comes amid an intensified manhunt following the November 11 attack on a CRPF post, in which two heavily armed terrorists opened fire, injuring three CRPF personnel.
Security forces had launched a cordon and search operation on Sunday in Khudwani and adjoining areas following intelligence inputs about the presence of terrorists suspected to be involved in the ambush. The operation was being supervised by senior Army officers, J&K Director General of Police Nalin Prabhat and Kashmir Range Inspector General of Police Sujit Kumar Singh.
Meanwhile, the bullet-riddled bodies of two Special Police Officers (SPOs), who had gone missing, were recovered from the remote Dachhan forest area of Kishtwar district on November 12.
Senior security officials have maintained that the operation will continue until those behind the CRPF patrol ambush are neutralised and the entire cordoned area is sanitised.

text_full:
2019
Every year, as winter approaches, parts of the Yamuna in Delhi begin to wear a thick blanket of white froth. The phenomenon is particularly visible near Kalindi Kunj and the Okhla Barrage, often around October-November. While the foam may look like soap bubbles floating on the river, it points to a deeper problem: the large quantities of pollutants entering the Yamuna. River watchers and experts say the phenomenon has been occurring for more than a decade.
2020
One of the primary reasons for the froth is surfactants and phosphates in wastewater. These substances are commonly associated with detergents and cleaning products used in households, laundry facilities, and industries. When wastewater containing these chemicals enters the river without adequate treatment, it adds to the pollutant load and creates conditions that encourage foam formation. A 2019 report submitted to the Yamuna Monitoring Committee identified high phosphate concentrations, largely from household wastewater, as a major contributor.
2021
Surfactants are compounds that reduce the surface tension of water, allowing air bubbles to form more easily and remain stable. When detergent-laden water is agitated, these compounds help produce layers of foam. Phosphate compounds present in wastewater can also settle in the riverbed and become suspended when the water is disturbed. The resulting turbulence brings the pollutants and air bubbles together, creating the white froth seen on the river's surface.
2022
Froth formation in the Yamuna begins after the monsoon, but becomes more visible as winter sets in. During this period, the river enters a lean-flow phase, when the volume of water is lower and there is less freshwater to dilute the pollutants entering it. Experts have also pointed to falling temperatures as a factor that makes the foam more persistent. This is why the phenomenon often becomes particularly noticeable around November, coinciding with Chhath Puja.
2023
The Okhla Barrage is an important part of the frothing process. Wastewater carrying detergents, surfactants, and other pollutants collects in the river before reaching the barrage. When water is released through the barrage gates, it falls from a height, creating turbulence and churning. This agitation brings pollutants settled in the water and riverbed to the surface, resulting in thick layers of foam downstream. The sudden release of water can therefore make the frothing more pronounced.
2024
The problem is not limited to household detergents. Untreated and partially treated sewage, industrial effluents, and wastewater from laundry and dyeing units also contribute to the pollution. A 2021 report by the National Green Tribunal-appointed monitoring committee noted that the 22-km stretch between Wazirabad and Okhla accounted for 76% of the Yamuna's total pollution load. Wastewater entering through drains from Delhi, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh adds to the burden on this stretch.
2025
A study by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI), reported by Hindustan Times in December 2025, identified another contributor: water hyacinth. As these plants decompose, they release natural compounds called saponins, which have foaming properties. The study found that these natural compounds, along with human-made surfactants from detergents, contribute to froth formation. When combined with the turbulence caused by water released through the Okhla Barrage, the foam becomes more pronounced.
2026
Removing foam from the river's surface does not address the pollution causing it. Defoaming agents and anti-surfactant solutions can temporarily suppress the froth, but the problem will persist as long as untreated sewage and industrial wastewater continue to enter the Yamuna.
The TERI study also flagged gaps in the ability of existing sewage and common effluent treatment plants to remove certain surfactants effectively. Ultimately, preventing pollutants from entering the river, improving wastewater treatment and ensuring adequate freshwater flow are essential to tackling the recurring frothing crisis.

text_full:
New Delhi: Swaraj Suiting Ltd reported a 94.5 percent year-on-year rise in standalone net profit to Rs 17.29 crore for the September quarter of FY27, as higher revenue lifted earnings at the integrated textile manufacturer.
Revenue from operations climbed 72.3 percent to Rs 219.52 crore from Rs 127.38 crore a year earlier, the company said in a statement. EBITDA grew 47 percent to Rs 41.2 crore, while earnings per share rose 62.1 percent to Rs 6.55.
First-Half Earnings
Revenue for the six months ended September 2026 almost doubled to Rs 402.89 crore, up 97.3 percent from Rs 204.17 crore in the same period last year. Net profit increased 96.9 percent to Rs 33.51 crore.
First-half EBITDA rose 46.8 percent to Rs 76.72 crore, while earnings per share increased 64.2 percent to Rs 12.69. The company generated Rs 40.59 crore in operating cash flow during the period.
Swaraj Suiting said EBITDA margins for both the September quarter and the first half were within its guided range of 18–20 percent, reflecting its current production capacity and product mix. The company said inventory gains had lifted margins in the corresponding periods of FY26, affecting year-on-year comparability.
Capacity Expansion
The company is expanding its spinning and finished fabric operations and investing in an advanced materials pilot project. It said the spinning investment and pilot project were progressing as planned, with commercial production targeted for the first quarter of FY28.
Separately, Swaraj Suiting plans to add around 30 million metres of annual finished fabric capacity across its denim and non-denim operations. The new capacity is expected to come on stream by the fourth quarter of FY28, taking total annual finished fabric capacity to about 73 million metres.
Renewable Energy Plans
The textile maker is also evaluating captive solar and wind power projects to improve energy security and reduce operating costs. It aims to meet up to 50 percent of its electricity requirements through in-house renewable generation by the end of FY28, subject to development of the proposed projects.
Swaraj Suiting manufactures denim and cotton finished fabrics as well as cotton yarn. Its operations span spinning, warping, yarn dyeing, weaving, fabric processing and finishing, covering several stages of production from yarn to finished fabric.

By Chang Dong-woo
MANILA, Nov. 16 (Yonhap) -- North Korea's nuclear weapons program is unlikely to feature prominently at an unprecedented summit among the leaders of the United States, China and Russia set to be held this week, though the gathering could provide a limited opening for renewed diplomatic contact between Washington and Pyongyang, U.S. experts said Monday.
U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are scheduled to hold their first-ever trilateral summit Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, where nuclear arms reduction is expected to be discussed.
Although Trump has previously expressed interest in meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong-un again, a U.S. administration official said last week that there are no plans for engagement with Pyongyang during the president's Asia trip.
The White House has not responded to a Yonhap News Agency inquiry on whether North Korea will be discussed during the trilateral summit.
Andrew Yeo, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said North Korea's nuclear program is unlikely to be discussed at the summit, citing considerable differences between Washington and Moscow over Pyongyang's nuclear ambitions.
 "Any mention of nuclear arms reduction from the three leaders will be a generally worded and vague statement," Yeo told Yonhap News Agency.
Ellen Kim, a senior fellow at the Korea Economic Institute of America (KEI), said the three leaders might briefly discuss North Korea behind closed doors, possibly at Trump's initiative, but other issues would likely take precedence.
"However, nuclear arms control among the U.S., Russia and China, along with the war in Iran, will likely take priority at the meeting," she said.
Scott Snyder, president and chief executive officer (CEO) of KEI, shared a similar assessment.
"I doubt that North Korea's nuclear program will be accepted as a discussion topic among the three leaders," Snyder said.
Despite the limited prospects for substantive discussions on North Korea, some suggest the summit could create an indirect opening for renewed diplomatic engagement between Trump and Kim.
Yeo said the trilateral meeting itself would not have much bearing on a Trump-Kim meeting but noted that Kim may consider a future meeting with Trump if he views the trilateral gathering positively.
Kim of KEI said the summit could, at best, help open diplomatic channels between Washington and Pyongyang, but is unlikely to lead directly to renewed engagement between Trump and the North Korean leader.
"Xi and Putin could convey Trump's messages to Kim," she said. "But they may be reluctant to support U.S.-North Korea negotiations for fear of losing their influence over North Korea."
Sydney Seiler, a former U.S. national intelligence officer for North Korea, suggested Xi and Putin could encourage Trump to continue reaching out to Pyongyang and consider incentives, including possible sanctions relief, without assuming a direct mediating role.
"It is most unlikely that either Xi or Putin is interested in taking a more active role in mediating a U.S.-DPRK summit," Seiler said, referring to North Korea by its official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The experts generally dismissed comparisons between the upcoming summit and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar international order without the participation of other countries directly affected by their decisions.
Robert Rapson, a former acting U.S. ambassador to South Korea, described such comparisons as misleading and said major differences among the three countries would make meaningful agreements difficult.
"Unlike Yalta, this meeting is not deciding the world order," Rapson said. "It's largely symbolic and performative, albeit not without some consequences."
Despite expectations of limited substantive results, Rapson warned that U.S. allies, including South Korea, should closely monitor the discussions to ensure their security interests are not compromised.
"As for allies and partners, including Seoul, they are somewhat out in the cold and will have to look to Trump's key senior advisers, to the extent possible, to keep them apprised of developments and to help ensure the president does not go off the rails with respect to their core interests," Rapson said.

title: Trump, Xi and Putin to meet at Shenzhen APEC summit
summary:
**📝****Three in Shenzhen****📝**

This Thursday, at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, **Donald Trump, Xi Jinping** and **Vladimir Putin** will meet for the first time. All three participants [confirmed](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/trump-xi-putin-ukraine-nuclear-tariffs-russia-iran-.html) the meeting: the White House, the Kremlin, and China as the host. Western media have already dubbed it "Yalta 2.0," though no one expects breakthroughs, including the participants themselves.

🔻**What do we know?**

▪️The APEC summit will take place on November 18–19, with 21 countries participating. Trump will arrive in Shenzhen on the evening of the 17th. On the 19th, he will first have a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi, and then, to conclude his visit, a three-way format with Putin. No separate bilateral Trump-Putin meeting is planned.

▪️The main topic for the Americans is nuclear arms reduction; they also promise to discuss the war with Iran. An American official called the meeting "the first conversation" between three nuclear powers and immediately clarified that no agreements will be reached. According to CBS and Chinese sources, Ukraine is not planned for discussion, __but who knows__.

▪️According to FT, **they decided not to coordinate the agenda in advance,** which is unusual for Xi, who prefers strictly regulated meetings. On November 9, the WSJ reported that Beijing wanted minimal discussion, while the US insisted on a free exchange of views. According to Dmitry Peskov, the sides proposed points that some considered priorities while others deemed inexpedient.

🖍The host of the meeting is the least interested in the noise around it. The Chinese have been cautious for a long time and avoid comparisons with "Yalta." Moreover, the three-way format risks linking China with so-called Ukraine and Iran, even though China's leadership tries not to play a central role in peace processes.

The nuclear issue is also uncomfortable for them: China's arsenal is many times smaller than Russia's and America's, and they have no desire to sit at the table "as equals" on restrictions. The American formulation that China should "take its place at the table of adults" illustrates this well.

🚩For Russia, the meeting is advantageous primarily for its status, and carries almost no risks: talking at one table with the leaders of the two largest economies is always useful. However, a "new Yalta," that is, a division of spheres of influence, will not happen here. Even if the conversation turns to so-called Ukraine, everything still comes down to the realities on the ground.

📌Nevertheless, the real result of Shenzhen is the precedent itself: the three largest nuclear powers will sit at one table, and a channel for discussing global problems and arms control has emerged that did not exist before.

Next, it's worth watching two things: whether China will agree to continue the format after November 19, and whether more problematic topics, like a new architecture for European security, will appear in it.

title: Sachin backs Jay Shah’s vision for cricket’s growth, wishes him success for second term as ICC Chair
summary: Digital Desk | New Delhi, Nov 16 (IANS) Legendary former India cricketer Sachin Tendulkar congratulated Jay Shah on taking up another term as International Cricket Council (ICC) Chair, highlighting his efforts towards expanding the game, strengthening its ecosystem and creating greater opportunities, particularly in women’s cricket. Sachin, widely regarded as one of the greatest batters in the history of the game, took to social media platform X to extend his wishes to Shah. “The growth of cricket depends on creating opportunities, strengthening the game’s ecosystem and taking it to newer audiences. @JayShah has worked hard towards these priorities, with particular emphasis on women’s cricket. Wishing him continued success as he takes on another term as ICC Chair." Shah was reappointed unopposed as the ICC Chair for a second term on Monday, with the global governing body’s Board confirming the decision during its meetings in Bali. The reappointment provides continuity in leadership as cricket prepares for its return to the Olympic Games at Los Angeles 2028, while pursuing wider global expansion, increased participation and commercial growth. Head of Cricket at National cricket Academy (NCA) VVS Laxman also extended his wishes to Shah. "Congratulations @JayShah on being re-elected as ICC Chairman for a second term. A proud moment and a reflection of your commitment to the game. Wishing you continued success as you lead world cricket into an exciting new era. Best wishes always." The ICC said Shah’s reappointment followed a proposal by the Board’s directors and reflected their confidence in his leadership at a significant stage in the sport’s development. Shah, now 38, was unanimously elected ICC Chair in August 2024, began his tenure on December 1, 2024, and became the youngest to hold the position at age 35. Before that, he headed the influential Finance and Commercial Affairs (F&CA) committee in the ICC. Shah’s rise to the ICC chair followed a long administrative path in Indian cricket. After serving as BCCI secretary from October 2019 to 2024, and earlier as joint secretary of the Gujarat Cricket Association (GCA) and President of the Asian Cricket Council (ACC), Shah has quickly become a key figure on the ICC’s decision-making panel, especially on revenue and commercial matters.

title: Trump ‘very positive’ on long-term friendship between India and US: IBM CEO
summary: Digital Desk | New Delhi, Nov 16 (IANS) Arvind Krishna, Chairman and CEO of IBM, said on Monday that President Donald Trump is very positive on the long-term friendship between India and the US, as well as confident in the Indian diaspora’s achievements. Answering an IANS question here during a roundtable interaction, Krishna said Trump has always been bullish on India and its diaspora. “He (Trump) is always very positive on the India-US relationship. He's very positive on the long-term friendship between the two countries. And look, in my presence and to me, he's always been very positive about the Indian diaspora that is there globally and in the United States,” Krishna told IANS. Krisna, along with India's Ambassador to the US Vinay Mohan Kwatra, renowned chef Vikas Khanna, entrepreneur Vishal Gondal, and US National Institutes of Health director, Jay Bhattacharya, joined the US President at the Diwali celebration in the Oval Office at the White House. The US President also recently praised IBM CEO for the company’s advances in semiconductor manufacturing. Trump has said that highly skilled Indian professionals are always welcome in the United States. “Highly skilled Indians will get more opportunities. India has very talented people,” he said on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Evian, France, in June this year. Meanwhile, India has secured an assurance from the United States that Indian goods will enjoy preferential market access in the American market compared to competing countries under the proposed bilateral trade agreement (BTA), Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Sunday. Goyal said the understanding was already reached at the leadership level when Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Trump agreed on a broad framework for strengthening bilateral trade ties. “This was already agreed between the leaders -- President Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi when they announced that we have both come to a broad framework agreement a few months ago, and it has been acknowledged that India will get preferential trade access in the US with lower duties than our competitor countries,” Goyal noted. India and the US had finalised the framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement in February, with both sides aiming to deepen economic engagement and expand market access. The two sides are currently working towards concluding the first tranche of the pact by the end of the current financial year.

बिलकिस बानो सामूहिक दुष्कर्म केस: दो दोषियों की उम्रकैद की सजा पर सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने लगाई रोक, जमानत भी दी
सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने बिलकिस बानो गैंगरेप और हत्या मामले में उम्रकैद की सजा काट रहे दो दोषियों को जमानत दे दी है। अदालत ने उनकी सजा पर रोक लगाते हुए कहा कि दोनों 17 साल से अधिक समय जेल में बिता चुके हैं और उनकी अपील में तथ्यों तथा कानून से जुड़े मुद्दों पर सुनवाई की जरूरत है।
विस्तार
जस्टिस एमएम सुंदरेश और जस्टिस प्रसन्ना बी वराले की पीठ ने 28 अक्तूबर को यह आदेश पारित किया। दोनों दोषियों ने बॉम्बे हाईकोर्ट के 2017 के फैसले को चुनौती दी थी। हाईकोर्ट ने उनकी दोषसिद्धि और सजा को बरकरार रखा था। दोनों दोषी उन 11 लोगों में शामिल हैं, जिन्हें गुजरात सरकार ने अगस्त 2022 में समय से पहले रिहा किया था। हालांकि, सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने 2024 में उनकी रिहाई के फैसले को रद्द कर दिया था।
17 साल से अधिक समय जेल में रहने का दिया हवाला
सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने अपने आदेश में कहा कि दोनों दोषी 17 साल से ज्यादा समय जेल में बिता चुके हैं। पीठ ने यह भी ध्यान दिया कि उनमें से एक गंभीर रूप से दिव्यांग है। अदालत ने कहा कि अपील में तथ्यों और कानून से जुड़े कई ऐसे सवाल हैं, जिन पर फैसला किया जाना बाकी है। इसी आधार पर पीठ ने दोनों की सजा निलंबित करने और जमानत देने का आदेश दिया।
दोषियों के वकील ने क्या दलील दी?
दोषियों की ओर से पेश वरिष्ठ अधिवक्ता सिद्धार्थ लूथरा ने अदालत को बताया कि दोनों 17 साल से अधिक समय से जेल में हैं। उन्होंने यह भी दलील दी कि एक आरोपी का नाम एफआईआर में दर्ज नहीं था और घटना के करीब तीन साल बाद उसे मामले में आरोपी बनाया गया था। वकील ने दूसरे दोषी की गंभीर दिव्यांगता का भी हवाला दिया।
सरकारी पक्ष ने जमानत का किया विरोध
अतिरिक्त सॉलिसिटर जनरल राजा ठाकरे ने जमानत याचिका का कड़ा विरोध किया। उन्होंने कहा कि निचली अदालत और हाईकोर्ट दोनों ने मामले से जुड़े सभी महत्वपूर्ण साक्ष्यों और तथ्यों पर विचार करने के बाद दोषियों को सजा सुनाई थी। उन्होंने अपराध की गंभीरता को भी जमानत का विरोध करने का आधार बताया।
हालांकि, सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने अपील में विचार किए जाने वाले मुद्दों और दोषियों के जेल में बिताए समय को ध्यान में रखते हुए सजा निलंबित करने का फैसला किया।
ट्रायल कोर्ट की शर्तों पर मिलेगी जमानत
सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने कहा कि दोनों दोषियों को संबंधित ट्रायल कोर्ट की ओर से तय की जाने वाली शर्तों के आधार पर जमानत दी जाएगी। मामले में उनकी अपील पर सुनवाई तय प्रक्रिया के अनुसार आगे होगी। अदालत ने स्पष्ट किया कि अपील में उठाए गए तथ्यों और कानूनी मुद्दों पर अभी फैसला होना बाकी है।

text_full:
Out and about: Against New Zealand, India's bowling was the silver lining
Led by Arshdeep Singh, the seam bowlers have strengthened India's one-day bowling pool by being effective but not identical.
There will be little appetite for appraisals in the India batting group in the aftermath of this ODI tour of New Zealand. Too many collapses, too many false shots, too many instances of promising starts dissolving into frustrating exercises for survival—India’s batting had very few reasons to cheer.
For a team trying to time how to peak ahead of the ODI World Cup, this series was a spanner in the works, exposing uncomfortable questions about India’s ability to negotiate difficult conditions away from home.
But cricket tours are also rarely remembered exclusively for what went wrong. Sometimes, the most important discoveries happen when a side is trying to survive its most uncomfortable moments. The batting was traumatic overall—Virat Kohli was the only Indian batter to cross fifty and the entire quota of fifty overs played out just once—but on the flip side, India’s bowling also offered an encouraging glimpse into the future.
The most immediate and obvious gain is Gurnoor Brar, whose imposing physical presence was matched by the hostility of his bowling, offering India a rare advantage away from home.
The consistency with which Brar tormented New Zealand’s top-order—Tim Seifert especially—was a throwback to the past when fast bowlers could bore batters with their discipline. Selection is no exact science and can be right only in hindsight. Brar’s progress however makes for a compelling insight into the benchmarks that need to be passed to make it to the team so close to an ODI World Cup.
From here, Brar—who has also been added to the Test squad—for South Africa seems a logical call, purely because of his aggression that is in sync with the conditions. The trampoline bounce in New Zealand should be replaced by slightly harder surfaces next year, making Brar the right candidate to rile batters even in the middle overs. And while Indian conditions would demand greater precision and the patience to construct spells when the ball is not doing much, right now that might not be required of him.
If Brar's appeal lies in his physicality, Anshul Kamboj is finally living up to the promise of staying economical without being passive, maintaining control to stay relevant with an easy, no-frills run-up. Five wickets spread across four outings, backed by a decent economy, Auqib Nabi effectiveness with the older ball also makes him an interesting proposition beyond conditions that favour conventional seam or swing.
It is perhaps premature to draw sweeping conclusions from one tour, but the important point is that Brar, Nabi and Kamboj have strengthened India’s bowling pool by not being identical. With Jasprit Bumrah being rested more than ever, this variety is exactly India’s bowling attack needs in the long run.
The most intriguing development, though, might be happening with Arshdeep Singh. Well established as India’s all-weather T20 spearhead, Arshdeep’s greatest strengths lie in his ability to swing the ball and execute yorkers. But this tour suggested the making of a more rounded fast bowler who adapts his methods to the demands of a particular match setting.
At the core of this effectiveness is the knack of hitting that length to which some batters play forward and others hang back. Sunday’s match offered a comprehensive view of that skill. From squaring up Will Young—just before he was induced into a wicket-taking pull—to foxing Dean Foxcroft with a scrambled seam delivery producing a thick edge to slip, Arshdeep tried to not conform to any particular template of bowling.
And that’s crucial considering the changing dynamics of one-day cricket. His use of the short ball was also particularly revealing. Attacking the body while making the batters guess his lengths, Arshdeep appeared more assured in sustaining pressure throughout the innings, rather than merely looking for breakthroughs with the new ball or at the death. Beyond Arshdeep’s match-winning haul at Mount Maunganui thus stood out his control, variety and match awareness brought upon by the responsibility of defending a sub-par score on a good track.
None of this should obscure India’s batting concerns though. The failure to build substantial partnerships, underlined by a vulnerability against disciplined seam bowling, means India’s batting strategy requires a serious probe.
The series was won alright but worrying is how this performance was fuelled nearly entirely by India’s seam bowlers. Perhaps that is going to be the more enduring legacy of this 3-1 series win. Travelling to New Zealand on the heels of a prolific run from the batters in the home series against West Indies, India were looking short of bowling edge. But now they leave having discovered that their white-ball fast-bowling future might be more exciting than previously imagined.
- Somshuvra Laha has been covering sports through chaos and calm since 2008, all while calling Hindustan Times home. Equally at ease decoding seam bowling at Lord's, spin at Eden Gardens or 4-4-2, he sees every match as a chance to dissect the game in unique ways.Read More

Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Monday said a large section of society remains deprived of government schemes as they were left out during previous census exercises, stressing the need to include all sections in the upcoming Census 2027, particularly the Musahar community in eastern UP.
Speaking at the launch of the self-enumeration process for Census 2027 in the state in Lucknow, Adityanath said, "Through my public engagement, I have observed that a large segment of society remains deprived of government schemes because they were overlooked during the census exercise. Since the very same data is later used to formulate these schemes, this group naturally remains deprived, especially the 'Musahar' community."
The chief minister said the Musahar community is among the most destitute sections of society and its members do not even possess legal ownership of the land on which their huts stand.
"Had they been honestly included in past censuses and their extreme distress discussed, then would this community still be on the brink of starvation, even after 70 years of Independence? This raises a serious question about the lack of sensitivity within our entire system," Adityanath said.
The chief minister further said, "Had we gathered correct information and drawn the government's attention towards their plight, they would have been recognised as rightful beneficiaries of state schemes, and action plans could have been formulated for them in the first Five-Year Plan."
As part of the second phase of the country's first digital census, the self-enumeration process will be conducted across Uttar Pradesh from November 16 to 30, 2026.

Malankara Orthodox Church expresses displeasure with govt over Patriarch's visit to Manarcad church
Kottayam , The Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church on Monday expressed displeasure with the state government over the visit of Patriarch of Antioch Ignatius Aphrem II to the Manarcad church, with Metropolitan Yohanon Mar Dioscoros alleging that a "strange legal advice" given to the government had caused a deep wound to the Church.
The remarks came a day after Jacobite Syrian Church head Moran Mor Ignatius Aphrem II, Patriarch of Antioch and Supreme Head of the Universal Syrian Orthodox Church, celebrated Holy Mass at St Mary's Cathedral in Manarcad despite objections from the rival Malankara Orthodox faction.
The latter had approached the Kerala High Court against the visit. The court had directed the State Police chief to ensure that the Patriarch did not violate visa conditions or Supreme Court directions in connection with the ongoing church dispute.
The Cathedral was managed by the Jacobite Syrian faction, even though the Malankara Orthodox Church claims it belongs to them.
The Patriarch left for Damascus on Monday after concluding his five-day visit to Keralam.
The dispute between the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Syrian factions concerns the ownership and administration of several churches in the state and has been the subject of prolonged legal battles.
Speaking at a function attended by Kerala Assembly Speaker Thiruvanchoor Radhakrishnan at Mooledam Church, Dioscoros said the Orthodox Church was prepared to make sacrifices in defence of its position.
"The Malankara Church has suffered a wound because of very strange legal advice. There is a need to heal that wound. Those who caused it should take the responsibility to heal it," he said.
Referring to Radhakrishnan, whom he described as someone he personally loved and respected, the Metropolitan said people should speak only good things.
"Everyone should understand that even if you throw a laddu, a throw is still a throw," he said, suggesting that hurtful remarks or actions did not become harmless merely because they were presented in pleasant words.
He said the Church was prepared to make sacrifices in defence of its position and beliefs.
Meanwhile, Baselios Joseph Catholicos Bava of the Jacobite Syrian Church said those alleging that he or the Patriarch of Antioch had violated court orders were free to approach the judiciary instead of blaming the government.
"If anyone has a complaint that the Patriarch or I have committed contempt of court, they can approach the court if they are convinced about it. There is no need to target the government. The government has only done what is right and what it had done earlier. The Patriarch has not done anything new," he said.
"If they believe that any court order has been violated, we will abide by the court order. That is all. It is very simple," he added.
He called for discussions between the two factions to explore a dignified resolution, including unity, separation or maintaining the status quo.
"There are several options. Whether it is dignified unity, dignified separation or maintaining the status quo, all these possibilities should be discussed. There are fundamental issues involving faith and authority that also need to be addressed," he said.
Speaker Radhakrishnan declined to comment on the state government's position on the dispute but said there was an impression that tensions were gradually cooling down.
"A judicial decision has been taken. Administrative decisions also need to follow," he said.
He said there were people keen on resolving the dispute and urged all sides not to aggravate the situation.
"Let the issue be resolved. We shouldn't add fuel to the fire and worsen the atmosphere," he said.

K'taka man claims GST registration in his name used for ₹350 cr transactions; police initiate probe
Ballari , An inquiry has been initiated into the complaint of a man who has alleged that a GST registration was opened in his name using his credentials without his knowledge and used to carry out transactions worth ₹350 crore, police said on Monday.
Roshan Jameel, a resident of Ballari, works as a service advisor at a car showroom and learnt about the alleged transactions only when GST officials visited his house recently for an inquiry, they said.
Subsequently, his family approached the the police with a complaint seeking registration of an FIR in the matter, police said.
Police have also written to GST officials seeking further details about the registration and the transactions carried out using the complainant's credentials.
"Yes, we have received a complaint. However, we are seeking the opinion of our legal adviser on whether an FIR can be registered based on the allegations made by the complainant and, if so, under which provisions. We have also written to GST officials seeking further details to advance the investigation," a senior police officer said.
The officer explained that, as per the prescribed procedure, the business entity's address, office and other details must be verified before a GST registration number is issued.
"In this case, we do not know what procedures were followed, and we do not have details of the person who allegedly impersonated the complainant. All these aspects are being verified," he said.
Speaking to a local TV news channel here, Jameel said he learned about the alleged misuse of his identity only after Central GST officials visited his house and informed his family about the transactions.
"I earn only ₹15,000 a month, and my father works as a daily-wage labourer. We have not conducted any business, nor were we aware that a GST number had been opened in my name," he said.
According to Jameel, the officials visited his house on Thursday using the address mentioned on his Aadhaar card and informed his family about the closure of the GST registration.
"My mother told them that I had gone to work. That was when we learned about the matter. We later made enquiries with the auditor and were told that transactions worth ₹350 crore had taken place in my name," he said.
He said neither he nor his family had received any messages or notifications regarding the GST registration or the transactions.
"We have filed a complaint seeking FIR registration and are waiting for further information from the police. We want a proper investigation and justice," he added.

text_full:
How did 'wire replacements' ground planes across entire US?
Sydney, On Friday, all flights across the United States were grounded for more than four hours due to what appeared to be a telecommunications issue.
The Federal Aviation Administration issued an alert citing "extraordinary circumstances" and called for all departing flights to remain ground stopped until further notice. According to media reports, about 3,500 flights were in the air when the alert was issued all landed safely.
With thousands of flights delayed and cancelled, millions of passengers were stranded in airports. The travel disruptions have been slowly resolving over the weekend.
Deep Dive
The ground stop was attributed to an update to air traffic control equipment during planned maintenance. So what exactly happened?
What caused it?
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the disruption to maintenance undertaken by government contractor L3Harris at a remote FAA facility.
The work involved replacing copper telecommunications wires with fibre-optic links, as well as changing how the system sends signals from an older method known as time-division multiplexing to the more recent internet protocol .
During this maintenance, a router reportedly generated more than 1,000 connection requests every four to five seconds. This affected other routers on the network, disrupting aircraft communications and some radar data feeds.
Duffy described the upgrade as a transition from analogue to digital technology, but this conflates different aspects of telecommunications.
Copper and fibre describe the physical medium carrying signals, while TDM and IP describe how information is transmitted and organised. Copper cables can carry digital data, and TDM is widely used in digital telecommunications. Fibre-optic systems also carry digital data, using light rather than electrical signals.
Consequently, replacing copper with fibre doesn't necessarily mean a change from analogue to digital.
The more significant change is the method for sending signals. With TDM, the system sends information through a single channel at fixed time slots, a bit like letting through traffic across a single-lane bridge at set intervals.
By contrast, an IP network can carry information in packets along many paths, which improves flexibility and how much data the network can handle.
However, it also changes how the equipment interacts and what can happen in case of a fault. If not isolated in time, a malfunctioning router can affect other equipment connected to the same network. On fibre, excessive connection requests will travel more freely.
Why would a network disruption ground planes?
-
Air traffic controllers use surveillance and radio communications to make sure planes travel smoothly and stay out of each other's way.
Radar and satellite-based surveillance provide aircraft positions, while communications allow controllers to issue instructions and coordinate movements between control centres.
All this relies on telecommunications networks connecting facilities across the country. Aircraft can navigate independently during a network failure, but controllers can't safely manage the usual volume of flights if the comms are not fully reliable.
The precise cause of why the router sent so many requests remains under investigation. Incorrect installation, configuration errors, and defective equipment are all potential explanations, and we'll have to wait and see.
A nationwide ground stop following a technical failure is not unprecedented. In January 2023, a malfunction of the FAA's Notice to Air Missions system, which supplies pilots with operational information, also suspended departures across the United States.
Although these two failures involved different systems, both show that a national aviation network that shares services throughout can be broadly impacted in case of a fault.
Was this related to Microsoft or AI?
The incident prompted speculation about it being linked to the global Microsoft outage that occurred just the day before.
Another suggestion was that the fault might lay with the FAA's recently announced expansion of SMART, an artificial intelligence-assisted traffic management system.
Both Microsoft and Air Space Intelligence, the company responsible for SMART, have denied involvement. Officials also noted that the maintenance of the network was completely separate from this air traffic control modernisation programme.
What can be done to prevent this happening again?
-
In September 2026, a US government report classified 51 of the FAA's 138 air traffic control systems as unsustainable, and another 54 as potentially unsustainable. The FAA is actively working on replacing ageing communications, radar, and control equipment.
However, modernisation introduces additional risks. When you add a new technology to the system, not only do you need to fit it with existing infrastructure, but you also need to maintain operations.
To prevent ground stops like the one this week, the FAA will need to do more than replacing cables or purchasing equipment. If they segment the network, faults won't travel as far. With proper configuration, they can ensure communications don't get overloaded if a similar router error were to happen.
The ground stop was a good measure to ensure safety when the comms failed. But a resilient aviation system must not only respond safely to equipment failures, but also prevent localised faults from disrupting national operations. FHK

How much is Amitabh Bachchan's Jalsa worth?
